column1: # What the Performance section of the root README charts: tools/readme/charts.py reads this file and benchmarks.tsv.
# Tab separated. Three kinds of line:
#     A chart, drawn once per OS that has data for it, to .github/assets/bench-<id>-<os>-{light,dark}.svg, in the
#     A row of a chart: the results of <benchmark> (Class.method) with exactly <params> (as benchmarks.tsv writes them,
#     the engine left out), measured by the workflow group <group>. <metric> is what the row compares: score (the JMH
#     score: an engine's time per operation, or the inverse of its throughput), a counter of benchmarks.tsv (bytes,
#     lower is better), or the difference of two counters, a-b. <label> is the row's title.
#     <metric> does not compare engines on <os> (ubuntu-latest, windows-latest or macos-latest): the rows that chart it
#     are left out of that OS's charts, with <reason> printed in their place, and no comparison uses it there.
# Every result of a group that no row charts is still listed in the README, under "Every other result of the <groups>
# workloads on <OS>", by its score and every counter it records (a workload that records memory by its counters only:
# each says its time is not what it measures); the lists of where another engine costs less than Ledger cover those
# results too. benchmark/README.md describes every workload.

column4: macOS counts the bytes the kernel charges to the process as written to disk, not the bytes passed to write calls, and it charges some engines far less than their files hold afterwards: LMDB is credited with a small fraction of the pages a history sync leaves in use. Writes that are on stable storage when the call returns: a session stored before a message is sent, a received message stored before it is acknowledged, a webhook delivery stored before it is answered.
